one_liner: Small C++ ROLZ + Huffman compressor (Baidu, archived) that compresses about 3x faster than zlib -6 with a better ratio.
what_it_does: libzling is a block compressor (16 MB input blocks) with its own .zlng stream format, shipped as a library plus a command-line demo. The API is two functions, baidu::zling::Encode(Inputter*, Outputter*, ActionHandler* = NULL, int level = 0) and Decode(Inputter*, Outputter*, ActionHandler* = NULL), driven through abstract Inputter/Outputter interfaces; only FILE*-based adapters are provided, so in-memory use means writing your own adapter. It is not zlib- or gzip-compatible.
how_it_is_fast: It uses order-1 ROLZ (reduced-offset Lempel-Ziv): for each preceding byte it keeps a 4096-entry bucket of recent positions with an 8192-slot hash, so a match is coded as a short bucket index instead of a full offset. Levels 0-4 only change match-search depth (2 to 16) and lazy-matching depth. Literals pass through a per-context move-to-front transform, and 256 KB ROLZ chunks are entropy-coded with two length-limited static Huffman tables (15-bit and 8-bit) and a two-level decode table with a 10-bit fast path. Its speed advantage is on the compression side, where it avoids zlib's longer match-chain search.
when_to_use: Offline or batch compression of text-like data (logs, enwik-style text, tarballs) where compression speed matters more than decompression speed and you control both ends of the format.
Replacing zlib -6 when you want roughly 3x faster compression and about 2.5 percentage points smaller output (29.72% vs 32.19% of silesia.tar in lzbench 2.4).
Studying or vendoring a compact ROLZ implementation (about 1,000 lines of C++ in src/) under BSD-3-Clause terms.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted input: AFL fuzzing found decompression crashes (issue #10, disclosed 2015), the coder was rewritten in 2018 after the 2015 fuzz fixes, and Decode() never checks its read position against the block's stated compressed length.
Big-endian targets: issue #12 reports round-trip data corruption on POWER8 ppc64, never fixed, and lzbench disables it on big-endian PowerPC.

Decompression-heavy workloads: lzbench 2.4 measures 183 MB/s decode against zlib -6 at 314 MB/s; zstd 1.5.7 -3 reaches 31.37% with 240 MB/s compression and 1151 MB/s decompression in lzbench's 4 MB-block one-thread table, which beats zling on decode by about 6x for a ratio within 2 points.
Anything needing gzip/zlib interoperability, streaming of small messages, or a maintained dependency: the repo is archived and the author points users to richox/orz.
Memory-constrained use: the encoder allocates a 16 MB input block plus about 10 MB of ROLZ buckets (256 x ~40 KB), and the decoder about 16 MB plus 4 MB.

integration.form: shared lib (build/CMakeLists.txt builds only a SHARED library plus the zling demo; the src/ files can also be dropped into a project)
integration.dependencies: none (bundles msinttypes headers for old MSVC)
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 2.8; the CMake file passes -std=c++14 although the code is C++98-style; lzbench had to add a missing <functional> include to build it
integration.platforms: little-endian only in practice (data corruption reported on big-endian ppc64); x86-64 is what the benchmarks cover; MSVC support was added in 2015
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; each Encode/Decode call allocates its own buffers and coder state, so separate calls on separate Inputter/Outputter objects share nothing visible in the source.

gotchas: The README sample calls Encode(&inputter, &outputter, level), but the third parameter is ActionHandler*; the real call is Encode(&in, &out, NULL, level).

Corrupt input makes Decode() throw std::runtime_error (bad flag, bad Huffman code, invalid block size), and allocation failures throw std::bad_alloc, so callers need exception handling. There is no checksum in the format.
A level outside 0-4 is not validated: the ROLZ encoder returns -1 and Encode() goes on writing a bogus block header.
The encoder silently drops to level 0 for any 256 KB chunk whose Huffman output exceeds 95% of its input, so throughput varies with how compressible the data is.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over zlib-ng or libslz only if you can accept a non-deflate format and want a better ratio from a fast compressor; for most new work zstd (better decode speed and a maintained, fuzzed codebase) or bzip3/libbsc (better ratio) are safer choices, and libzling's successor richox/orz is not catalogued here.
verified_claims_summary: lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, one thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.2 GHz, silesia.tar) measures zling -0 at 86.1 MB/s compression and 183 MB/s decompression with output 29.72% of input, against zlib 1.3.2 -6 at 26.8 / 314 MB/s and 32.19%: about 3.2x faster compression and 0.58x the decode speed. The author's README run on a Xeon E5-2620 v3 shows enwik8 compressed by e0 in 2.208 s versus gzip's 6.502 s (31.46 MB versus 36.52 MB output), with decode at 1.043 s versus 1.089 s.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit 2018-10-12, archived 2021-04-26 with a pointer to richox/orz, and lzbench labels it 'not recommended for production use (per author)'. The BSD-3-Clause text sits in the source headers (there is no LICENSE file), so it can be copied, but it should be fuzzed and hardened before any use on external data.
